entry.title: Does It Work? A Verifier for Coding Agents, the Results, and What We Learned

link.title: Does It Work? A Verifier for Coding Agents, the Results, and What We Learned

entry.content:
Accuracy on the tricky Q&A test after each stage, from our training logs. Pre-training creeps up to about 52%, mid-training jumps past 65% in its first 42 steps, and post-training ends at 70.8%. The dashed lines are the CLM authors' published numbers.

Introduction

Over the last four posts we built a decision model from scratch: a frozen Qwen3-8B that turns any text into an embedding, two small heads that map states and options to vectors of dimension 512, a contrastive loss that teaches them to put each state next to its right option, and three stages of training. The result is a single checkpoint, our general post-training checkpoint. This post asks the only question that matters: does it work?

We test it in three ways, each closer to real use than the last. The first is a held-out set of tricky questions, where every right answer comes with up to ten wrong answers designed to look right. The second is the job decision models were made for in coding: a coding agent attempts the same task several times, and the model must pick the attempt to keep. The third is a game played in real time, where the model has about 17 milliseconds per decision.

In every test, we compare our checkpoint with the released CLM-8B1, the model we set out to replicate, and whenever we could, we ran both ourselves on exactly the same data. Remember from part 4 that our checkpoint was chosen with a rule fixed in advance, on development data only. None of the numbers below played any part in choosing it.

The last part of the post is about what we learned. Some lessons are about decision models, but the most useful ones are about the tests themselves.

Test 1: tricky questions

The first test reuses the two chunks of question-and-answer pairs that were held out from training, the ones with hard negatives. For each of their 191,161 questions, the model sees the right answer and that question’s hard negatives, up to ten wrong answers generated to be close to it, and must rank the right one first. The score is the share of questions where it does, the top-1 accuracy. A model that guesses at random gets about 10%, since a question has about nine hard negatives on average.

Checkpoint Ours CLM-8B (published)
After pre-training 51.6% 52.1%
After mid-training 68.1% 69.2%
After post-training 70.8% 68.5%

Our run follows the published one closely through the first two stages, about half a point and one point below. Post-training is where the two diverge. CLM-8B’s post-training costs it a little accuracy on these questions, while ours gains almost three points. We also measured the released CLM-8B checkpoint ourselves on the same 191,161 rows and got 68.6%, in line with the published number, so the comparison is fair.

The interesting part is the shape of the curve in the opening animation, which comes straight from our training logs. During pre-training, the heads become very good at the in-batch task they are trained on: by the end, they pick the right answer among 1,024 candidates from other questions about 83% of the time. Yet on the tricky test, accuracy creeps from 44% at step 4,000 to 52% at step 29,000. The heads learn to tell a question about planets from a question about cooking, but not Mercury from Venus.

Mid-training changes this almost immediately. After only 42 steps, about four minutes on our GPU, tricky accuracy jumps from 51.6% to 65.2%, a gain that 25,000 steps of pre-training could not produce. The remaining 500 steps add three more points. This is the curriculum of part 4 at work: the broad geometry learned in pre-training is what lets the hard negatives teach so fast, and the hard negatives are where the precision comes from.

Post-training then adds 2.7 points, even though none of its four sources is new Q&A data. Part of it comes from the Q&A replay, which keeps the hard negatives in the loss, and part from the other sources: choosing between close actions in one environment and ranking two answers to the same instruction are, after all, the same skill.

A verifier for coding agents

The second test is the one decision models were built for. A coding agent, given a task, writes code, runs commands and reads their output, step after step, until it believes it is done. Its success varies from one attempt to the next, so a common strategy is to let it make several attempts and keep the best one. This is called best-of-N. At deployment there are no hidden tests to tell which attempt is right, so the choice needs a verifier: a model that looks at each attempt and says how promising it is2.

A decision model is a natural verifier, because an agent’s attempt is exactly the kind of data it was trained on. Every step of the attempt is a decision: the state is everything that happened before the step, and the action is what the agent did. The model scores each step, and the score of the attempt is the average over its last 12 steps:

\[\text{score}(\text{attempt}) = \frac{1}{12}\sum_{t=T-11}^{T} s\,\mathbf{u}_t\cdot\mathbf{v}_t\]

where \(T\) is the number of steps in the attempt, \(\mathbf{u}_t\) and \(\mathbf{v}_t\) are the state and action vectors of step \(t\) produced by the two heads, and \(s\) is the scale. Each term is the familiar score of part 1, how well the action fits its state. The attempt with the highest score is kept. Scoring every step rather than only the final answer is the idea behind process reward models3, and the last 12 steps are where an attempt either converges on a fix or goes in circles.

Best-of-four verification. Every step of every attempt gets a score, the last 12 are averaged, and the attempt with the highest average is kept. Only then do the task's tests say whether it passed. The scores are illustrative.

The DeepSWE benchmark

The CLM authors released a benchmark for this, which they call DeepSWE: 113 coding tasks, each attempted several times by a coding agent, with every attempt marked as passing or failing by the task’s tests, and all the steps already embedded with Qwen3-8B. The tasks are split into 75 for training and 38 held out, and on each held-out task the verifier picks one of up to four attempts. A task counts as resolved if the picked attempt passed.

The protocol also adapts the model to this kind of data before testing. Starting from the checkpoint being tested, a short fine-tuning run trains the heads contrastively on the steps of the passing attempts of the training tasks, 22,576 steps from 66 tasks, with the authors’ own scripts and settings, which we ran unchanged. A model trained on what successful attempts look like tends to give lower scores to the steps of failing ones, which repeat themselves, revert changes or drift away from the task. The fine-tuning run depends on a random seed, so the whole procedure is repeated with five seeds and the results are averaged.

Intuition

Think of a coach who has to bet on one of four runners after watching only the last lap of each. He has never seen this race before, but he has watched thousands of good runners finish. A runner who finishes like those, steady and in control, is a better bet than one who is weaving and slowing down. The coach does not know who will win, and sometimes the steady runner falls on the last step. But averaged over many races, betting on the finish that looks most like a winner’s beats betting at random.

Results: read the ceiling first

Before looking at any score, look at what the test allows. Of the 38 held-out tasks, 21 are resolved by every attempt, and 4 by none. On those 25 tasks, the verifier’s choice cannot change anything. Only the 13 remaining tasks have both passing and failing attempts, so every verifier, good or bad, lands between 21 and 34 resolved tasks. Picking an attempt at random resolves 28 on average, and a perfect verifier would resolve 34.

The 38 held-out DeepSWE tasks. Only the 13 grey ones can tell verifiers apart, so every result lies between 21 and 34, with a random pick at 28.
Verifier Seeds 1234, 1, 2, 3, 4 Mean resolved, out of 38
Random pick   28
Ours, after the verifier fine-tuning 29, 30, 32, 30, 31 30.4
CLM-8B, after the verifier fine-tuning 31, 32, 30, 31, 31 31.0
Perfect pick   34

CLM-8B comes out ahead by 0.6 tasks on average. That is less than the spread between seeds of the same model, which goes from 29 to 32 for ours, and it is played out on 13 tasks, where one task is worth more than two and a half percentage points. The honest summary is a near tie, with a slight edge to CLM-8B. Measured from a random pick, ours closes 40% of the gap to a perfect verifier, and CLM-8B half of it.

We also tried both checkpoints directly, without the verifier fine-tuning: both resolve 27 tasks, one fewer than a random pick. On this benchmark, a general decision model is not a useful verifier out of the box. It needs the short adaptation to what passing attempts look like, which is cheap, since everything is already embedded.

A second coding test

DeepSWE is small, so we added a test from outside the CLM release: 95 held-out issues from SWE-bench Verified4, a standard benchmark of real GitHub issues, each with up to 15 attempts by coding agents, taken from a public dataset of embedded attempts. The metric is the expected best-of-four success: for every possible group of four attempts on an issue, the verifier picks one, and we average whether it passed. Here both checkpoints are used directly, without any fine-tuning.

Verifier Expected best-of-four success
Random pick 70.7%
CLM-8B 69.4%
Ours 71.3%
Perfect pick 83.3%

Ours is ahead of CLM-8B by about two points, but look at the random pick again: ours is only 0.6 points above it, and CLM-8B is below it. Without adaptation, neither model is a strong verifier for these attempts. As we will see in the lessons, a head trained on this kind of data does much better.

Test 3: a game in real time

The CLM release comes with a demonstration that puts decision speed to the test: a side-scrolling runner game, where a dinosaur has to jump over or duck under obstacles. Each course lasts 60 seconds, and the model makes about 3,300 decisions per course, one every 18 milliseconds or so. Our checkpoint answered in about 17 ms per decision (median), on par with CLM-8B, which is the speed part 1 promised.

One decision in the game. The state describes what is ahead, and each option comes with the planner's note about it. If the model proposes an unsafe action, the shield replaces it with the most probable safe one. The descriptions and probabilities are illustrative.

At each decision, the game builds a state, such as “Dino runner game. Cactus ahead, 120 px away.”, and three options, jump, duck and run. A built-in planner works out which actions are safe and which is best, and its notes are written into each option’s text: “Safe. … Best.” for its preferred action, “Unsafe. … Collision.” for the dangerous ones. The model picks the option with the highest probability. A shield then checks the choice: if the model proposed an unsafe action, it executes the most probable safe action instead.

Two numbers describe a run. Planner agreement is the share of decisions where the model’s proposal has the same effect as the planner’s choice, measured before the shield acts. Survival counts the courses finished without a single crash. We ran both checkpoints on five fresh courses, with the shield on:

Checkpoint Planner agreement Courses survived Shield interventions
CLM-8B 66.9% 5 / 5 4,956
Ours 36.1% 5 / 5 3,083

CLM-8B follows the planner far more often. Ours agrees with it only about a third of the time, yet proposed an unsafe action less often: the shield had to step in 3,083 times for ours, against 4,956 for CLM-8B. In other words, our model often picks a safe action that is not the planner’s favourite, like running instead of jumping when both are fine. Both survive every course with the shield. Without it, our checkpoint is not a good player: on the five original courses of the demonstration, it crashed 45 times and finished none without a crash.

This game is the test where CLM-8B is clearly better, and also the one where the numbers need the most care, as the lessons will show.

The full picture

Test Ours CLM-8B Random Perfect
Tricky Q&A, top-1 accuracy 70.8% 68.6% ≈ 10% 100%
DeepSWE, resolved out of 38, with verifier fine-tuning 30.4 31.0 28 34
DeepSWE, resolved out of 38, used directly 27 27 28 34
SWE-bench Verified, expected best of four 71.3% 69.4% 70.7% 83.3%
Game, planner agreement with the shield on 36.1% 66.9%    
Game, courses survived with the shield on 5 / 5 5 / 5    

Our decision model, built from public data and recipes we reconstructed ourselves, matches CLM-8B on the coding benchmark it was designed for, beats it on tricky questions and on the external coding test, and falls behind on following the game’s planner. The whole general post-training study, including encoding its new data and running all these evaluations, cost about \$2.85 of GPU time.

What we learned

Know the floor and the ceiling

The most important number in any benchmark table is often the one that is missing: what a random choice would score. On DeepSWE, 25 of the 38 tasks are decided before the verifier even looks at them, a random pick already resolves 28, and the difference between the two models is a fraction of a task. On SWE-bench, a random pick beats one of the two models. Without those two reference points, “31.0 against 30.4” or “71.3% against 69.4%” look like results. With them, they look like what they are: small differences on a narrow margin.

A benchmark can contain its own answer

The game’s options carry the planner’s notes, and the planner’s favourite option literally ends with the word “Best.”. A model that learns to look for that word scores perfectly on planner agreement without understanding anything about the game.

We checked this. We trained a specialist head on 8,640 planner-labeled decisions from other courses, adjusting only the action head. It reached 100% planner agreement on fresh courses, against 66.9% for CLM-8B, and the shield had to intervene only 206 times. It looks like a triumph. But with the shield off, it crashed on every one of the five courses. It had learned to read the label, not to play. Planner agreement on this prompt measures how well a model follows a hint written in its options, which is worth knowing, but is not the same as making good decisions.

Specialists win their benchmark and lose the others

We also trained a coding specialist: starting from an earlier post-trained head, it learned to prefer passing attempts over failing ones on 318 SWE-bench issues, kept separate from the 95 test issues. On the SWE-bench test, it reached 74.0% expected best-of-four success, by far the best result, almost three points above our general checkpoint. On DeepSWE, it fell to 28.8, below every other head we tested. The gain did not transfer from one set of coding tasks to another. This is why the checkpoint we report is the general one, chosen with no benchmark in sight: it is never the best at one test, but it holds up on all of them.

Hard negatives are where the precision comes from

The opening animation is the clearest result of the whole project. Pre-training on 62 million pairs taught the heads to find the right answer among 1,024 random ones, but left them guessing between close alternatives. Forty-two steps on hard negatives did more for that than the last 25,000 steps of pre-training. And keeping the hard negatives in the replay during post-training is what let our final checkpoint keep improving on them, where CLM-8B’s post-training lost a little.

Fix the selection rule before looking

With dozens of candidate checkpoints and half a dozen benchmarks, it is easy to fool oneself by keeping whichever checkpoint looks best on the tests. We fixed the selection rule of part 4, on development data only, before running any benchmark, and stuck to it even where a different choice would have looked better on one test. The results above are less flattering than a hand-picked table would be, but they are the ones a new task would likely see.

Frozen embeddings make experiments cheap

Because the language model is frozen and every text is embedded once, the cost of an idea is the cost of training two small heads. Our pre-training run, 30,000 steps on 62 million pairs, took two hours on one GPU. Mid-training reached its best checkpoint in 21 minutes. Each post-training recipe took minutes and cost cents. That is what made it possible to compare recipes side by side, on identical batches, and to throw away the ones that did not work.

What we would do next

The weak point of our checkpoint is the gap between “plausible” and “best”: it proposes dangerous actions less often than CLM-8B, but it often disagrees with the planner on which safe action is better. More preference data, where two good options must still be ranked, is the most direct fix. On the coding side, the verifier only ever learns from passing attempts. Training it on pairs of passing and failing attempts, as the coding specialist did, but on a broader mix of tasks, should keep the specialist’s gains without its brittleness. And for evaluation, we would want coding benchmarks with many more mixed tasks, and game prompts that describe the situation without labelling the answer.

Conclusion

A decision model is a simple idea: let a frozen language model read, let two small heads compare, and replace generation with a cosine. Over this series we built one from scratch: we embedded once, trained with a contrastive loss, followed a three-stage curriculum from 62 million questions to agents and preferences, and tested the result against the model we set out to replicate. It answers in 17 milliseconds, it can be retrained for cents, and on the tests that measure what it was trained for, it holds its own against CLM-8B.

The code is in the repository. If you want to see a decision model built step by step on video, the Vizuara AI walkthrough is a great companion to this series. Thank you for reading.

References

  1. J. Kwok, H. Kang, T. Suresh, J. Saad-Falcon, M. Pavone, C. Ré and A. Mirhoseini. CLM-8B (project page) and its code, including the DeepSWE benchmark and the game. ↩

  2. K. Cobbe et al. Training verifiers to solve math word problems. arXiv:2110.14168, 2021. ↩

  3. H. Lightman et al. Let’s verify step by step. International Conference on Learning Representations, 2024. arXiv:2305.20050 ↩

  4. C. E. Jimenez et al. SWE-bench: can language models resolve real-world GitHub issues? International Conference on Learning Representations, 2024. arXiv:2310.06770 ↩
entry.summary: Our decision model against the released CLM-8B: tricky questions, choosing between a coding agent's attempts, and a game played in real time. And the lessons, including the ones the benchmarks taught us about themselves.

entry.title: Training a Decision Model: The Data, and Pre-, Mid- and Post-Training

link.title: Training a Decision Model: The Data, and Pre-, Mid- and Post-Training

entry.content:
The three stages, with the data each one trains on and two examples of it. Each stage starts from the best checkpoint of the previous one. The examples are illustrative, except the two post-training questions, which come from our data.

Introduction

The previous post gave us the learning machinery: a batch of pairs, a similarity matrix, the InfoNCE loss, a learned temperature and hard negatives. A loss, however, is only half of training. The other half is what the model sees, in which order, and how we decide that a checkpoint is good enough to keep.

The heads are trained in three stages. Pre-training teaches them, from scratch, to put 62 million questions next to their answers. Mid-training sharpens them on a smaller set of questions that come with tricky wrong answers. Post-training turns them toward what a decision model is actually for: agents choosing their next action, and judging which of two answers is better.

This post follows that path from the data on disk to the last checkpoint. We start with the data and how it reaches the GPU, go through the three stages one by one, and spend the most time on the last one: the general post-training recipe that gave our final checkpoint. The results themselves are the subject of part 5.

The data

62 million question-and-answer pairs

The first two stages train on question-and-answer pairs from NVIDIA’s Nemotron-CC v2.11, a large pretraining corpus built from web pages. It includes a subset called High-Quality-DQA: short STEM questions with their answers, which the language model Qwen3-30B-A3B wrote from high-quality science and technology web documents, following the “diverse QA” recipe of the original Nemotron-CC2. Each document gives several pairs, which is why the same-document mask of part 3 is needed.

The CLM authors3 took these pairs and, as we saw in part 2, released them not as texts but as embeddings: they ran every question and every answer through the frozen Qwen3-8B. That is the version we train on. There are 62.45 million pairs, each a state embedding and an action embedding of shape (4096,), stored in half precision.

The pairs are cut into chunks of 100,000, about 625 in total, spread over six shards. A chunk is three files: the 100,000 question vectors, the 100,000 answer vectors, and a small table that records which document each pair came from, the doc_id that the same-document mask of part 3 needs. Each vector file has shape (100000, 4096) and weighs about 0.8 GB, so a chunk is about 1.6 GB and the whole dataset about 1 TB.

The first shard, shard_00, also has hard negatives: for each pair, up to 10 wrong answers that the CLM authors generated with Gemini to be close to the right one, then embedded like everything else, stored as a file of shape (100000, 10, 4096), with a second file that counts how many of the 10 slots are real. That is about 8.2 GB per chunk and 0.25 TB in all, for about 3 million pairs and 26.7 million hard negatives, roughly 9 per pair.

Four chunks are set aside and never trained on, the same four the authors held out: two ordinary chunks, shard_05/0083 and 0084, to measure the in-batch loss, and two chunks with hard negatives, shard_00/0028 and 0029, to measure how often the right answer beats its tricky alternatives. Of their 200,000 pairs, 191,161 have at least one hard negative, and this is the “tricky Q&A” test that comes back in part 5.

Feeding a terabyte to one GPU

All our training ran on a single GPU, an NVIDIA L40S with 48 GB of memory, in a machine with 256 GB of ordinary memory (RAM). The Q&A data, about 1 TB, sits on a network disk. So the data is four times larger than the RAM, and twenty times larger than the GPU’s memory: it can never be loaded all at once. It has to be brought in piece by piece, and in a way that never leaves the GPU waiting.

Two facts shape the solution. The first is that a training step is fast: the heads are small, so the GPU finishes a batch of 16,384 pairs in a fraction of a second. Reading from the disk is slow by comparison: loading a single 1.6 GB chunk takes far longer than a step. If every batch were read straight from the disk, the GPU would spend most of its time idle. The second is that a batch should mix pairs from all over the data, so that the wrong answers it provides for free are varied.

The solution is a small pipeline with two workers running side by side, a reader and a dealer, and a buffer of data in RAM between them, called a pool.

The reader loads 24 chunks into a pool in RAM. The dealer shuffles the pool and sends it to the GPU batch after batch, one training step per batch, until every pair has been used once. Then it reshuffles the same pool and goes through it again, three times in all, while the reader loads the next pool.

The reader picks 24 chunks, in a random order that changes every epoch, loads them from the disk and joins them into one pool: 2.4 million pairs, about 39 GB of RAM.

The dealer then shuffles the pool, meaning it puts its 2.4 million pairs in a random order, and cuts that order into consecutive batches of 16,384 pairs. A pool of 2.4 million pairs gives 146 batches (the few pairs left over at the end wait for the next shuffle). The dealer sends these batches to the GPU one after another, and each one is one training step: the GPU computes the loss on the batch, and the heads are updated, before the next batch arrives. After 146 steps, every pair of the pool has been used exactly once. This is one pass over the pool.

Only then does the dealer shuffle the same pool again. The new random order puts every pair in a different batch, next to different neighbours, so it meets different wrong answers than in the first pass. The dealer cuts it into 146 new batches and sends them one after another, as before. It does this three times in total, so one pool gives 3 × 146 = 438 training steps. For the first pool:

Pool Pass Training steps
1 (chunks 1–24) 1st shuffle 1 to 146
1 2nd shuffle 147 to 292
1 3rd shuffle 293 to 438
2 (chunks 25–48) 1st shuffle 439 to 584

Meanwhile, the reader has not been idle. As soon as it handed over the first pool, it started loading the next 24 chunks, so the second pool is usually ready by the time the dealer finishes with the first one, and the GPU moves on without waiting. Reusing each pool three times, with a fresh shuffle each time, is what gives the reader enough time to do this.

Two queues connect the workers, and both are kept small: at most one finished pool waits for the dealer, and at most a few batches wait for the GPU. However large the dataset, RAM never holds more than three pools at once: the one being dealt, one waiting, and the one being loaded, about 120 GB.

Over a whole epoch, the 621 training chunks make 26 pools, so an epoch is about 11,300 steps, and every pair is seen three times, each time in a different batch. Our pre-training run stops at 30,000 steps, a little over two and a half epochs.

Stage 1: pre-training

Pre-training starts from two randomly initialized heads and trains them on every chunk except the four held-out ones, with the symmetric InfoNCE loss and the same-document mask of part 3. There are no hard negatives yet: every wrong answer comes from the batch.

The optimizer is AdamW4 with no weight decay, gradients are clipped to a norm of 1, and the temperature starts at 0.07 and is learned. The learning rate is constant, and its value comes from a simple scaling rule:

\[\eta = \eta_0 \sqrt{\frac{1024}{w}} \sqrt{\frac{B}{1024}} = 0.002 \times \sqrt{\frac{1024}{1536}} \times \sqrt{16} \approx 0.00653\]

where \(\eta\) is the learning rate, \(\eta_0 = 0.002\) is a base rate for a reference setup with layers of width 1024 and batches of 1024, \(w = 1536\) is the width of the heads’ hidden layers, and \(B = 16{,}384\) is the batch size. The first factor lowers the rate for wider layers, where each update moves the output more. The second raises it for larger batches, whose gradients are less noisy and can be trusted with larger steps. The square root, rather than a straight proportion, is the rule that works for Adam-style optimizers5.

Every 1,000 steps, the trainer measures the in-batch loss on the two held-out ordinary chunks. Whenever this loss is the lowest so far, the weights are saved as the stage’s best checkpoint. If nine evaluations in a row bring no improvement, training stops early; otherwise it stops at 30,000 steps. A second checkpoint, overwritten at every evaluation, holds the weights together with the optimizer and the step counter, so a run that crashes resumes exactly where it was.

At this stage the heads learn the broad geometry of questions and answers: a question about planets lands near answers about planets, a question about cooking near answers about cooking. As we saw in part 3, the loss falls from its chance level of about 9.7 to about 1.9 within 8,000 steps.

Stage 2: mid-training

Mid-training starts from the best pre-training checkpoint and adds the hard negatives. Only shard_00 has them, so this stage trains on its 28 non-held-out chunks, about 2.8 million pairs. Each state’s hard negatives become extra columns in its row of the similarity matrix, exactly as in part 3.

A few settings change with the data. The learning rate drops to 0.001, because the heads are no longer random and need adjusting rather than building. Pools hold 6 chunks instead of 24, since a chunk with its hard negatives is about 10 GB, and each pool is shuffled once. An epoch is now only about 168 steps, so the trainer evaluates every 42 steps, four times per epoch, and this time it keeps the checkpoint with the lowest loss on the hard-negative held-out chunks. Our best mid-training checkpoint came at step 546, a little over three epochs in.

Why not use hard negatives from the start? One reason is practical: they exist for fewer than 5% of the pairs, so pre-training on them alone would throw away most of the data. The other is that they are only useful once the model knows the basics. To a random model, every answer is equally confusing, and the subtle difference between a right answer and an almost-right one is lost in the noise. Training on easy examples first and harder ones later is an old idea called curriculum learning6, and it is what the split between pre- and mid-training does.

Intuition

Think of a medical student. In his first years, he reads the whole library: anatomy, chemistry, hundreds of diseases, without going deep into any of them. That is pre-training. Then come the exam questions written to trap him, where two diagnoses fit the symptoms and only a detail separates them. These would have been useless in his first week, when everything was new, but now they are exactly what he needs. That is mid-training. What remains is the residency, where he applies all this to real patients, which is what post-training does for our model.

Stage 3: post-training

After mid-training, the heads are very good at one task: matching a question with its answer. A decision model has to do more. An agent’s state is a long history of commands and outputs, its options are actions rather than answers, and sometimes the question is not “which option is right?” but “which of these two is better?”. Post-training adapts the heads to these situations.

Our first post-training run reproduced the original recipe: about 847,000 agent decisions, filling 60% of each batch, with the other 40% replayed from the Q&A chunks with hard negatives, for 400 steps. It was a useful baseline, but it left two problems. The first is the wrong answers. In a batch that mixes dozens of agent datasets, the wrong actions for a shopping state are mostly shell commands, SQL queries and household moves, which the model can reject at a glance, so the batch says little about what a decision model most needs: telling apart two actions that both make sense in the situation. The second is that the only signal is “this is what the agent did”. Nothing ever says that one option is better than another, which is what a verifier or a judge needs.

The recipe we kept, and the one the rest of this post is about, addresses both. It produces a single general checkpoint, trained without any benchmark data, that learns from four sources at every update.

One update of post-training: four sources, each with its own loss, added with fixed weights.

The total loss is

\[\mathcal{L} = 0.25\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{terminal}} + 0.25\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{Q\&A}} + 0.20\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{env}} + 0.30\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}}\]

where each term is the loss of one source, described below, and the weights say how much each source counts in an update. Each source comes with its own data, and its own way of preparing it.

Terminal steps

The first source is coding agents working in a terminal, from the LiteCoder dataset7. Its authors already turned each trajectory into (state, action) steps and ran them through the same Qwen3-8B, so the embeddings come ready to use, and encoding them cost us nothing. There are 278,817 training steps, and 4,096 steps from separate tasks are kept for development. Each update samples 256 training steps and applies the ordinary InfoNCE loss of part 3, with steps of the same task masked from each other, like pairs from the same document.

Q&A replay

Training only on new data would make the heads forget what they learned about questions and answers, a well-known problem called catastrophic forgetting8. The usual remedy is replay9: keep mixing in some of the old data. Each update draws 128 Q&A pairs, with their hard negatives, from 24,576 rows taken from three shard_00 chunks. Keeping the hard negatives matters: replaying plain pairs would protect the broad geometry of pre-training, but let the sharpness of mid-training fade. A fourth chunk provides a separate development sample, and none of these chunks is a held-out test chunk.

Choices within an agent environment

The third source fixes the problem of easy wrong answers. It uses four environments from ADP v210, a collection that converts many public agent datasets into one format: a household simulator, a web shop, a database and a knowledge graph11. Each one is a set of trajectories, the full record of an agent solving a task: the task, then a sequence of agent messages and tool calls, each followed by what the environment returned.

Every agent message is a decision. The history before it is the state, and the message itself, with its tool call, is the action.

Each agent message in a trajectory is a decision, so each one gives a pair: the state is everything that happened before it, and the action is the message itself, with its tool call written as name(arguments). The pairs of one trajectory overlap heavily, since the state of step 6 contains the whole state of step 4, so at most 6 random pairs are kept per trajectory. Histories longer than 2,000 characters keep their first 480, where the task is stated, and their last 1,500, the most recent steps. Pairs whose state was already seen, and empty actions such as “OK.”, are dropped.

The trajectories are split by goal: a hash of the task’s instruction sends one goal in five to development, so the model is always tested on goals it has never trained on, and two runs of the same task never end up on both sides. Each environment contributes up to 640 training pairs and 160 development pairs.

The key step is choosing the wrong answers. For each pair, the model must pick the recorded action among 8 options, where the 7 others are actions recorded for other goals in the same environment. A shopping state is now compared with other shopping actions: searches for other products, clicks on other buttons.

Against actions from other environments, the right one wins without effort. Against seven actions from other shopping goals, the model has something to learn. The scores are illustrative.

The loss is the cross-entropy of this 8-way choice:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{env}} = -\log \frac{e^{s\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}^{+}}}{e^{s\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}^{+}} + \sum_{m=1}^{7} e^{s\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{d}_m}}\]

where \(\mathbf{u}\) is the state vector, \(\mathbf{v}^{+}\) the recorded action, \(\mathbf{d}_1, \dots, \mathbf{d}_7\) the seven distractors, all three produced by the heads, and \(s\) the frozen scale. It is the InfoNCE row loss of part 3 with a hand-picked set of wrong answers instead of the batch. Each training pair gets four different draws of distractors, and each update takes 16 examples from each environment, so no environment dominates.

One caveat: another goal’s action is not always wrong for this one. Two shopping tasks can both start with a sensible search. This source measures how well the model retrieves the recorded action, which is a useful signal but not a perfect one.

Answer preferences

The fourth source teaches the heads to judge. It comes from UltraFeedback12, a dataset in which several models answered the same instructions, and AI annotators gave each answer a fine-grained score and a written critique. From six of its source files we took 320 training and 64 development instructions each, 1,920 and 384 in all, split by a hash of the instruction’s text. For each instruction, we keep the highest- and the lowest-rated answer, provided their scores differ by at least one point, together with their two critiques. How the heads learn from them is the subject of the next section.

Embedding once

Apart from the terminal steps, all these texts are new: environment states and actions, instructions, answers and critiques. They are embedded once, with the same frozen Qwen3-8B and the same last-token recipe as everything else, and cached as half-precision vectors. Every training run afterwards reads the cache, so it only ever trains the heads, and trying a new recipe costs minutes rather than hours.

Learning from preferences

The preference loss deserves its own section, because it is the one new idea of this stage. Take the instruction “Describe the capital of Spain in 25 words.” The higher-rated answer describes Madrid, though in 17 words instead of 25. The lower-rated one says that Santo Domingo is the capital, of the Dominican Republic. The model should score the first one higher.

The difference between the two answers' scores, the margin, goes through a sigmoid to become a probability. The critiques give a second margin, which also serves as a soft target for the first.

The score of each answer is the usual one, its cosine with the instruction times the scale, and what matters is the difference:

\[m_a = s\,(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}^{+} - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}^{-}), \qquad P(\text{better} \succ \text{worse}) = \sigma(m_a) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-m_a}}\]

where \(\mathbf{u}\) is the instruction’s state vector, \(\mathbf{v}^{+}\) and \(\mathbf{v}^{-}\) are the action vectors of the higher- and lower-rated answers, \(m_a\) is the answer margin, and \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid, which turns any number into a probability between 0 and 1. A margin of 0 means the model cannot tell the two apart, \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\). A large positive margin means it is confident that the better answer is better. This way of turning a difference of scores into a probability of preference is the Bradley–Terry model13, the same one used to train the reward models of chat assistants14. The loss is \(-\log \sigma(m_a)\), the cross-entropy of a two-way choice, which pushes the margin up until the model is confident.

The critiques add a second view of the same comparison. The critique of the good answer reads like praise with small reservations; the critique of the bad one points out a factual error. We score both critiques against the instruction, exactly like answers, which gives a critique margin \(m_c = s\,(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{c}^{+} - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{c}^{-})\), where \(\mathbf{c}^{+}\) and \(\mathbf{c}^{-}\) are the action vectors of the two critiques. The full preference loss is

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}} = -0.45\log\sigma(m_a) - 0.45\log\sigma(m_c) + 0.10\,\mathrm{BCE}\big(m_a,\ \sigma(m_c)\big)\]

where the first two terms ask both margins to favour the better side, and the third is a binary cross-entropy that asks the answer margin to match the confidence of the critique margin:

\[\mathrm{BCE}\big(m_a,\ t\big) = -\,t \log\sigma(m_a) - (1 - t)\log\big(1 - \sigma(m_a)\big), \qquad t = \sigma(m_c)\]

where \(t\) is the soft target, a probability rather than a hard 0 or 1. The target is treated as a constant: no gradient flows back through it, so this term moves the answer margin toward the critiques and never the reverse. Learning from another model’s probabilities rather than from hard labels is the idea behind knowledge distillation15; here the “teacher” is the critique view of the same heads. When the critiques make a clear case, the answer margin is pushed to be confident too; when the two critiques are close, it is not pushed to an extreme.

The critiques are only used in training. At serving time, the model sees an instruction and candidate answers, exactly like any other decision.

Intuition

Picture an apprentice judge at a cooking contest. After each round, he is told which of two dishes the panel scored higher, and that alone teaches him something. But he is also given the panel’s written notes on each dish. The notes tell him why one dish won, and how clear the verdict was: “a slight lack of salt” and “burnt and inedible” are very different reasons to lose. A judge who reads the notes learns not only to pick the winner, but also how sure to be.

Training and choosing the checkpoint

Post-training starts from our mid-training checkpoint at step 546. Each update uses AdamW at a learning rate of 0.00008, gradients clipped to 1, and the temperature frozen.

The runs are small enough that we could compare recipes side by side, with identical batches and the same random seed, so that any difference comes from the recipe alone. The first round trained two versions for 320 updates: one with the answer margin only, one with the answers and the critiques. The first round’s winner was then continued for 320 more updates at half the learning rate, 0.00004, again in two versions: one with the ordinary same-environment distractors, and one where, on every other update, three of the seven distractors are mined, chosen as the actions the current heads find most similar to the state. Each round also tried the average of the late checkpoints of both versions, a cheap trick that often helps16.

With this many candidates, the choice of the final one matters as much as the training, and it is easy to fool oneself by picking whichever looks best on the benchmarks. So the selection rule was fixed before looking at any benchmark, and it only uses development data: held-out terminal steps, a Q&A sample from a chunk not used in training, development goals of the four environments, and development instructions of the preference data.

The rule compares each family to the mid-training checkpoint with the relative error reduction:

\[r = \frac{a - a_0}{1 - a_0}\]

where \(a\) is the candidate’s accuracy, \(a_0\) the mid-training checkpoint’s accuracy, and \(1 - a_0\) the errors that were left to fix. Going from 90% to 95% halves the remaining errors, \(r = 0.5\), while going from 50% to 55% only fixes a tenth of them, \(r = 0.1\). This puts families with very different accuracy levels on the same scale. The score is the average of \(r\) over the four families, with the answer accuracy counting twice as much as the critique accuracy inside the preference family. Two conditions guard against forgetting: a candidate is only eligible if its terminal-step accuracy is at least as high as mid-training’s, and its Q&A accuracy at most 0.5 points lower. The mid-training checkpoint itself is eligible, so a recipe that makes things worse is never kept.

Under this rule, the critique version beat the answer-only version in the first round, with a development score of 0.24 against 0.20. In the second round, the ordinary distractors beat the mined ones, 0.30 against 0.28, and in both rounds the weight average scored lower than the best single run. The final checkpoint is therefore the plain one: answers with critiques for 320 updates, then 320 more with ordinary same-environment distractors, 640 updates in all. Mining hard distractors, which sounds like the obvious next step after part 3, did not help here, perhaps because two goals in the same environment already provide confusable actions, and mined ones are more often actions that would be correct too.

Since everything is embedded once, these runs are very cheap. The two training sweeps cost about \$0.04 of GPU time combined, and the whole general post-training study, including encoding the new texts and running all the evaluations, cost about \$2.85.

Implementation

All the stages share one training loop in the repository, and each stage only changes its data and its validation score. Here is the dealer of the data pipeline: for each pool, it shuffles, cuts the shuffled order into batches and sends them one by one, and repeats this as many times as configured:

def _deal_batches(self) -> None:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(self.settings.seed)
    batch_size = self.settings.batch_size
    while (pool := self._get(self.pools)) is not END:
        for _ in range(self.settings.pool_repeats):
            shuffled = rng.permutation(pool.num_rows)
            # Rows left over after the last full batch are skipped; each shuffle skips different ones.
            for start in range(0, pool.num_rows - batch_size + 1, batch_size):
                # Sorted indices read memory in order, which makes the copy faster.
                rows = np.sort(shuffled[start : start + batch_size])
                if not self._put(self.batches, pool.take(rows)):
                    return
    self._put(self.batches, END)

One post-training update draws from the four sources and adds their losses with the weights above. The environment choices are rows of 8 action indices, the recorded one first, scored against their state and trained with an ordinary cross-entropy whose target is column 0:

agent_loss = sample_loss(train, 256, rng)
qa_loss = sample_loss(replay, 128, rng)
pref_rows = train_rows[rng.choice(len(train_rows), 64, replace=False)]
answer, review = margins(model, vectors, pref_rows)
distractors = mined if recipe == "continued_mined" and step % 2 else train_choices
sampled = np.concatenate([choices[rng.integers(len(choices), size=16)]
                          for choices in distractors.values()])
logits = choice_logits(model, actions, torch.as_tensor(sampled, device=device))
domain_loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, torch.zeros(len(logits), device=device, dtype=torch.long))
loss = (0.25 * agent_loss + 0.25 * qa_loss + 0.20 * domain_loss +
        0.30 * preference_loss(answer, review, recipe != "answer_only"))

The preference loss is three lines, with softplus(-m) standing for \(-\log\sigma(m)\) and detach() making the critique margin a constant target:

def preference_loss(answer, review, use_reviews):
    if not use_reviews:
        return F.softplus(-answer).mean()
    # The critique supplies a second supervised view and a soft target for the answer-only view.
    teacher = review.detach().sigmoid()
    return (0.45 * F.softplus(-answer).mean() + 0.45 * F.softplus(-review).mean()
            + 0.10 * F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(answer, teacher))

And the selection score is the relative error reduction, averaged over the four families:

def selection_score(metrics, baseline):
    # Equal weight for the four data families. Normalize each gain by remaining errors.
    def error_reduction(metric):
        return (metrics[metric] - baseline[metric]) / max(1e-6, 1 - baseline[metric])
    preference = (2 * error_reduction("answer_preference") + error_reduction("review_preference")) / 3
    return (preference + error_reduction("agent_top1") + error_reduction("qa_top1") + error_reduction("action_macro")) / 4

What’s next

We now have a trained decision model: heads pre-trained on 62 million pairs, sharpened on hard negatives, and post-trained with a general recipe on terminal steps, agent environments, Q&A replay and answer preferences with critiques. What remains is the question that matters: how good is it? Part 5 puts it to the test on the tricky Q&A set, on choosing between coding agents’ attempts, and in a game that needs decisions in milliseconds, compares it with the released CLM-8B, and looks back at what worked, what did not, and what we would do differently.

entry.title: Contrastive Learning: InfoNCE, Temperature and Hard Negatives

link.title: Contrastive Learning: InfoNCE, Temperature and Hard Negatives

entry.content:
A batch of five (state, action) pairs. Every state is compared with every action, the right answers sit on the diagonal, and each row and each column becomes a small classification problem.

Introduction

In the first post we built the decision model: a frozen Qwen3-8B that turns every text into an embedding, and two small heads that map states and actions to vectors of dimension 512, whose cosine is the score. In the second post we saw why the language model stays frozen, and how the embeddings are computed once and stored.

What we have not seen is how the heads learn. When training starts, they are random networks: the vector of “Which planet is closest to the Sun?” lands somewhere on the sphere, and the vector of “Mercury” lands somewhere else, with no reason to be close. Training has to move them together, and move “Mars” away.

The surprising part is what the training data looks like. It contains only matching pairs: a question and its right answer, an agent’s state and the action it took. Nobody labeled the wrong answers. This post is about how a model can learn to reject wrong answers it was never shown, a family of methods called contrastive learning, and about the three ingredients that make it work for us: the InfoNCE loss, the temperature, and hard negatives.

Wrong answers for free

The idea is simple. Training goes through the data in batches, and our batches are large: 16,384 pairs at a time. Inside a batch, every pair has its own right action, and the actions of the 16,383 other pairs are, almost always, wrong answers for it. The answer to a question about planets is a wrong answer to a question about cooking. So every batch provides, for free, 16,383 wrong answers for each state.

Contrastive learning turns this into a training signal: for each state, push its vector toward its own action and away from all the other actions in the batch. The model never needs to be told what is wrong; it learns by contrast with what is right.

The similarity matrix

Let’s write it down. Take a batch of \(B\) pairs. The state head turns the \(i\)-th state into a normalized vector \(\mathbf{u}_i\), and the action head turns the \(j\)-th action into a normalized vector \(\mathbf{v}_j\), both of dimension 512. Stacking them gives two matrices, \(U\) and \(V\), each of shape \((B, 512)\).

Comparing every state with every action gives a matrix of scores:

\[Z = s \, U V^\top, \qquad z_{ij} = s \, \mathbf{u}_i \cdot \mathbf{v}_j = s \cos\theta_{ij}\]

where \(Z\) has shape \((B, B)\), \(z_{ij}\) is the score of state \(i\) against action \(j\), \(s\) is the learned scale from part 1, and \(\theta_{ij}\) is the angle between the two vectors. Because both vectors have length 1, their dot product is the cosine of that angle.

This one matrix product does all the work. With \(B = 16{,}384\), it computes about 268 million scores at once, which a GPU does in a fraction of a second. The right answers are on the diagonal: entry \(z_{ii}\) compares state \(i\) with its own action. Everything off the diagonal compares a state with someone else’s action.

InfoNCE: a classification over the batch

Now read the matrix one row at a time. Row \(i\) holds the scores of state \(i\) against all \(B\) actions, exactly the situation of part 1: one state, a list of options, and a softmax that turns scores into probabilities. The only difference is that the options are the actions of the batch, and we know which one is right, the \(i\)-th. So each row is a classification problem with \(B\) classes, and we can train it with the usual classification loss, the cross-entropy:

\[\mathcal{L}_i = -\log p_i^{+}, \qquad p_i^{+} = \frac{e^{z_{ii}}}{\sum_{k=1}^{B} e^{z_{ik}}}\]

where \(p_i^{+}\) is the probability the model gives to the right action of state \(i\) (the \(+\) marks the right answer), \(z_{ii}\) is the score of that right action, the denominator adds up the exponentials of all \(B\) scores in row \(i\), and \(\mathcal{L}_i\) is the loss of row \(i\). The loss is small when \(p_i^{+}\) is close to 1, that is, when the state’s own action stands out from all the others, and it grows quickly as \(p_i^{+}\) drops: \(-\log 0.9 \approx 0.1\), but \(-\log 0.01 \approx 4.6\). In the animation, state 2 gives its own action a probability of 0.90, so its loss is \(-\log 0.90 \approx 0.11\).

This loss is called InfoNCE1, from “noise-contrastive estimation”: the other actions in the batch play the role of noise that the right answer has to be told apart from. Averaging over the rows gives the loss of the batch, read from the states’ side:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{rows}} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} -\log \frac{e^{z_{ii}}}{\sum_{k=1}^{B} e^{z_{ik}}}\]

which is the row loss \(\mathcal{L}_i\) averaged over the \(B\) states of the batch.

Both directions

The matrix can also be read by columns. Column \(i\) holds the scores of action \(i\) against every state, and asks the mirror question: which state does this action belong to? The same loss, written for columns, is

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{columns}} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} -\log \frac{e^{z_{ii}}}{\sum_{k=1}^{B} e^{z_{ki}}}\]

where the denominator now runs down column \(i\): \(z_{ki}\) is the score of state \(k\) against action \(i\). Our loss is the average of the two:

\[\mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\mathcal{L}_{\text{rows}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{columns}}\right)\]

where \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{rows}}\) reads the matrix from the states’ side and \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{columns}}\) from the actions’ side.

This symmetric version is the one CLIP2 uses to match images with captions. Reading both directions gives each head two kinds of signal: a state must beat the other actions, and an action must beat the other states, so neither head can cheat by placing all its vectors in one corner of the sphere.

Intuition

Picture a hall with 16,384 people, each holding a question, and a table with 16,384 answer cards. Each person has to find the card that answers his question, and each card has to be claimed by the right person. Nobody ever tells a person which cards are wrong; he only learns, after each round, which one was his. Over many rounds, people get better at telling their card apart from the others, and the cards that look alike are the ones that teach the most.

What the gradient does

To see how the heads actually learn, we need the derivative of the loss with respect to each score: it says how much the loss changes when that score goes up a little. Training uses gradient descent, which moves every value by a small step in the direction that lowers the loss, that is, against the sign of its derivative:

\[z_{ij} \leftarrow z_{ij} - \eta \, \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_i}{\partial z_{ij}}\]

where \(\eta\) is the learning rate, a small step size, and \(\leftarrow\) means “is replaced by”. A positive derivative means that raising the score would raise the loss, so the update lowers the score; a negative derivative means the opposite. (In practice the update is applied to the weights of the heads, which then change the scores, but the direction is the same.)

For the row loss, the derivative has a remarkably clean form:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_i}{\partial z_{ij}} = p_{ij} - \mathbf{1}[j = i], \qquad p_{ij} = \frac{e^{z_{ij}}}{\sum_{k=1}^{B} e^{z_{ik}}}\]

where \(p_{ij}\) is the probability the model gives to action \(j\) for state \(i\) (the right action’s \(p_i^{+}\) is the case \(j = i\)), and \(\mathbf{1}[j = i]\) is 1 for the right action and 0 for the others.

Now plug the two cases into the update. For the right action, the derivative is \(p_i^{+} - 1\), which is negative, so the update raises its score by \(\eta \, (1 - p_i^{+})\): the less sure the model is, the stronger the pull. For a wrong action, the derivative is \(p_{ij}\), which is positive, so the update lowers its score by \(\eta \, p_{ij}\): the more probability a wrong action steals, the harder it is pushed down. Take row 2 of the opening animation. The right action has a probability of 0.90, action 3 has 0.10 and action 1 only 0.001 (shown as 0.00). One step raises the right score by \(0.10\,\eta\), lowers action 3 by the same amount, and leaves action 1 almost where it is: the model already knows it is wrong.

The same reasoning applies to the state vector itself:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_i}{\partial \mathbf{u}_i} = s \left( \bar{\mathbf{v}}_i - \mathbf{v}_i \right), \qquad \bar{\mathbf{v}}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{B} p_{ij} \mathbf{v}_j\]

where \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}_i\) is the average of all the actions weighted by their probability, the action the model currently expects for state \(i\), \(\mathbf{v}_i\) is the right action and \(s\) is the scale. The update \(\mathbf{u}_i \leftarrow \mathbf{u}_i - \eta \, \partial \mathcal{L}_i / \partial \mathbf{u}_i\) therefore adds \(\eta \, s \, (\mathbf{v}_i - \bar{\mathbf{v}}_i)\) to the state: a small step along the arrow that goes from the expected action to the right one. The state moves toward its own action and away from the actions it currently confuses with it, and when the model is already sure, \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}_i\) is almost \(\mathbf{v}_i\) and the step is almost zero.

Gradient steps on the circle. The right action is pulled toward the state, and each wrong action is pushed away in proportion to its probability, so the closest one moves the most.

The animation shows these forces on a circle: the wrong action closest to the state has the highest probability and is pushed the hardest, while the far ones barely move. In real training, the heads change rather than the points themselves, and states move as well as actions, but the forces are the same.

This also explains a weakness. Once most wrong answers in a batch are far away, their probabilities are all close to 0, and the batch stops teaching. We will come back to this with hard negatives.

Why bigger batches help

With \(B\) actions in a row, a model that knows nothing gives each the same probability, \(1/B\), and its loss is \(\log B\). For our batches, that is \(\log 16{,}384 \approx 9.7\): the loss at chance level. In our pre-training run, the loss was down to about 1.9 after 8,000 steps.

Larger batches help for two reasons. The first is that a harder test is a more informative one: picking the right answer among 16,384 is a much stronger statement than picking it among 16. Van den Oord and colleagues made this precise1: the InfoNCE loss gives a lower bound on the mutual information between states and actions,

\[I(\text{state}; \text{action}) \geq \log B - \mathcal{L}_{\text{rows}}\]

where \(I(\text{state}; \text{action})\) is the mutual information: how much knowing the state reduces our uncertainty about which action goes with it. It is 0 when the state says nothing about the action, and it grows as the state pins the action down. It is measured in nats, the unit of the natural logarithm, which is also the unit of the loss. \(\log B\) is the chance-level loss from above and \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{rows}}\) is the row loss. So the further training pushes the loss below chance level, the more shared information the heads are guaranteed to have captured. Since the loss can never go below 0, the bound can never exceed \(\log B\), so a larger batch lets the loss measure, and reward, more of what the two share. The second reason is the one from the gradient: the more wrong answers a batch contains, the more likely it is to contain a few close ones, which are the ones that teach. Contrastive methods like SimCLR3 and CLIP rely on very large batches for exactly this reason, and it is why being able to afford batches of 16,384, as we saw in part 2, matters so much.

Same-document masking

There is one catch in the “wrong answers for free” idea. Our question-and-answer data was built from documents, and a single document usually produces several questions. Two questions about the same article can easily have answers that fit both. Counting one as a wrong answer for the other would punish the model for being right.

So, before the softmax, we mask them: if pairs \(i\) and \(j\) come from the same document, with \(i \neq j\), we set \(z_{ij} = -\infty\). Since \(e^{-\infty} = 0\), that action simply disappears from the denominator of row \(i\), and it is neither rewarded nor punished. The diagonal is never masked: a pair’s own action always stays the right answer. The last part of the opening animation shows this for two pairs from the same document.

Temperature

The scale \(s\) deserves a closer look, because it shapes training as much as it shapes the final probabilities. It is often written as an inverse temperature, \(s = 1/\tau\), a name borrowed from physics: a high temperature spreads probability evenly, a low temperature concentrates it on the best option.

The same five cosines turned into probabilities with three different scales. With s = 1 the model can never be confident; at the cap, s = 100, a small difference in cosine decides everything.

Cosines only range from -1 to 1, so without a scale the scores are too close together for the softmax to ever be confident, as the animation shows at \(s = 1\). Multiplying by \(s\) stretches the differences. But too large a scale too early would make the model confident before it knows anything, with very sharp, unstable gradients. The answer, borrowed from CLIP, is to learn \(s\).

We store it as a logarithm, \(s = e^{t}\) with \(t\) the trained parameter, so that it can never become negative, and start it at \(\tau = 0.07\), that is \(s \approx 14.3\). As the heads improve and the right answers stand out, the loss can be lowered further by raising \(s\), so training raises it. To stop it from growing without limit, it is capped at 100. In our pre-training run, the scale had climbed to between 85 and 89 by step 8,000. In post-training we freeze it, because the CLM-8B checkpoints after mid-training and after post-training have the same scale.

Intuition

Think of \(s\) as the contrast setting of a photograph. With the contrast too low, everything is the same shade of grey and you cannot tell the objects apart. Turned up, the differences pop out. Turned up too far, every small difference becomes black or white, and you lose detail. Learning \(s\) lets the model turn the contrast up at the pace its knowledge allows.

Hard negatives

Back to the weakness we saw in the gradient. After a while, the in-batch wrong answers are mostly easy: a question about planets against answers about cooking, football and tax law. Their probabilities are close to 0, they stop teaching, and the model can reach a low loss while still confusing answers that are only slightly wrong. A model that knows “Mercury” fits a question about planets better than “lasagna” has not yet learned that it fits better than “Venus”.

Hard negatives fix this. For each question, the dataset provides a few wrong answers chosen to be close to the right one: plausible, on topic, but wrong. These were generated with Gemini and embedded by the people who released the data, up to \(k = 10\) per pair, for a subset of about 2.8 million pairs. Mined hard negatives are a standard tool in retrieval4 and contrastive learning5.

Each state gets up to k extra wrong answers of its own, appended to its row. States with fewer than k have their empty slots masked, and the extra answers only extend the rows.

In the loss, each state’s hard negatives become extra columns in its own row. Write \(\mathbf{n}_{i,1}, \dots, \mathbf{n}_{i,c_i}\) for the hard negatives of state \(i\), passed through the action head like any other action, where \(c_i \leq k\) is how many state \(i\) actually has. The probability of the right action becomes

\[p_i^{+} = \frac{e^{z_{ii}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{B} e^{z_{ij}} + \sum_{m=1}^{c_i} e^{s \, \mathbf{u}_i \cdot \mathbf{n}_{i,m}}}\]

where the first sum runs over the in-batch actions, as before, and the second over the state’s own hard negatives. Since some states have fewer than \(k\) hard negatives, the empty slots are filled with \(-\infty\), which removes them from the sum exactly like the same-document mask.

Hard negatives only extend the rows. They belong to one state each, so there is no sensible column for them: “which state does this wrong answer belong to?” has no answer. The column loss stays as it was.

The effect is large. The test that measures it, which we will use throughout the series, asks the model to pick the right answer among its own hard negatives on held-out questions. In the published CLM numbers, accuracy on that test goes from about 52% after the first training stage, without hard negatives, to about 69% after the second, with them.

Intuition

Hard negatives are the difference between two multiple-choice exams. In the first, the wrong options are absurd: “Which planet is closest to the Sun? Mercury, lasagna, the Eiffel Tower.” You can pass it without knowing any astronomy. In the second, the options are Mercury, Venus and Mars, and you actually have to know. A student who only ever takes the first kind of exam will feel confident and learn very little. The in-batch negatives are the first exam; hard negatives are the second.

Implementation

Here is the loss as it is written in the repository. The in-batch logits are one matrix product, followed by the same-document mask:

def in_batch_logits(embedded: EmbeddedBatch) -> torch.Tensor:
    """[rows, rows]: row i scores state i against every action. Pair i's own action is column i."""
    logits = embedded.scale * embedded.states @ embedded.actions.t()
    same_doc = embedded.doc_ids[None] == embedded.doc_ids[:, None]
    same_doc.fill_diagonal_(False)  # keep each pair's own action
    # Another pair from the same document is probably a fine answer too, so don't count it as wrong.
    return logits.masked_fill(same_doc, float("-inf"))

The hard negatives arrive as a tensor of shape \((B, k, 512)\), one row of \(k\) wrong answers per state. Each state is compared only with its own, and the empty slots are masked using the count of each row:

def hard_negative_logits(embedded: EmbeddedBatch) -> torch.Tensor:
    """[rows, k]: each state against its own hard negatives. Empty slots are -inf."""
    logits = embedded.scale * torch.einsum("rd,rkd->rk", embedded.states, embedded.hard_negatives)
    slot = torch.arange(logits.shape[1], device=logits.device)
    return logits.masked_fill(slot[None] >= embedded.negative_counts[:, None], float("-inf"))

The loss reads the matrix both ways. The columns use the in-batch matrix as is; the rows get the hard negatives appended, when the batch has them. In both cases, the right answer for row (or column) \(i\) is index \(i\), which is what targets says:

def contrastive_loss(embedded: EmbeddedBatch) -> torch.Tensor:
    logits = in_batch_logits(embedded)
    targets = torch.arange(len(logits), device=logits.device)
    # Read by column: for each action, which state is its own?
    action_to_state = F.cross_entropy(logits.t(), targets)
    # Read by row: for each state, which action is its own? Hard negatives are extra wrong actions for that row.
    if embedded.hard_negatives is not None:
        logits = torch.cat([logits, hard_negative_logits(embedded)], dim=1)
    state_to_action = F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)
    return (state_to_action + action_to_state) / 2

Finally, the scale lives in the model, stored as a logarithm and capped:

# Stored as a log so exp() keeps the scale positive. scale = 1 / temperature.
self.log_logit_scale = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(math.log(1 / loss.initial_temperature)))
self.max_logit_scale = loss.max_logit_scale

def logit_scale(self) -> torch.Tensor:
    return self.log_logit_scale.exp().clamp(max=self.max_logit_scale)

What’s next

We now have the whole learning machinery: pairs, a batch, a similarity matrix, a symmetric InfoNCE loss with a learned temperature, a mask for pairs that share a document, and hard negatives for the answers that are almost right. What remains is the data itself and the order in which the model sees it. Part 4 follows the training from start to finish: the 62 million question-and-answer pairs and how they are fed to the GPU, the three training stages, pre-, mid- and post-training, and the post-training recipe that worked best.

  4. V. Karpukhin et al. Dense passage retrieval for open-domain question answering. Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2020. arXiv:2004.04906 ↩

  5. J. Robinson, C.-Y. Chuang, S. Sra and S. Jegelka. Contrastive learning with hard negative samples. International Conference on Learning Representations, 2021. arXiv:2010.04592 ↩
